title: Residential Senior Care Franchises
one_liner: Franchised residential senior care is a fast-growing assisted-living niche driven by aging Baby Boomers, dementia care demand, higher senior-housing occupancy and tight new supply.
overview: The industry covers franchised outlets that provide residential housing, meals, supervision and help with activities of daily living for older adults, excluding pure home-care providers and facilities focused solely on inpatient nursing or rehabilitation. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline reported $6.0 billion of revenue and forecast $9.0 billion by 2026, implying a narrow 2025 franchise market of about $8.3 billion on that forecast path. Current 2025-2026 conditions support continued growth: the U.S. 65+ population reached 64.6 million in July 2025, Alzheimer's prevalence reached 7.2 million Americans age 65+ in 2025, senior housing occupancy ended 2025 at 89.1%, and assisted-living occupancy reached 87.7%. The main constraint is not demand but execution: labor availability, wage inflation, state licensing, development costs and the ability of residents to pay private monthly rates that reached a 2025 national median of about $6,200 for assisted living.

key_stats.market_size: $8.3 billion in 2025 estimated narrow U.S. franchised residential senior care revenue; $9.0 billion in 2026 based on the 2021 IBISWorld forecast path
key_stats.growth: 8.6% CAGR forecast for 2021-2026 in the baseline; broader U.S. Elderly & Disabled Services market growth was 3.4% in 2025
key_stats.senior_population: 64.6 million U.S. residents age 65+ in July 2025, up 16.2% from April 2020
key_stats.occupancy: Senior housing occupancy in NIC MAP primary markets ended 2025 at 89.1%; assisted living occupancy was 87.7% in Q4 2025
key_stats.pricing: 2025 national median assisted-living cost was about $6,200 per month, or $74,400 per year
key_stats.dementia_demand: 7.2 million Americans age 65+ were living with Alzheimer's dementia in 2025
key_stats.locations: Baseline forecast called for 4,070 franchised establishments by 2026, up from 2,746 in 2021

baseline_2022.market_size: $6.5 billion in 2022 estimated from the 2021 IBISWorld revenue base of $5.967 billion and the 2021-2026 forecast CAGR
baseline_2022.growth: About 8.6% in 2022 on the baseline forecast path

how_it_makes_money.resident_fees: Monthly private-pay charges for room, board, supervision, meals, housekeeping, medication support and activities of daily living assistance.
how_it_makes_money.care_level_add_ons: Higher fees for memory care, incontinence care, mobility support, night supervision, medication management and other higher-acuity services.
how_it_makes_money.entrance_or_community_fees: Continuing-care and some senior-living models charge upfront entrance or community fees in addition to recurring monthly fees.
how_it_makes_money.government_payments: A smaller share comes from Medicare- or Medicaid-related payments for qualifying medical or waiver-covered services; the baseline cited 15.7% of 2021 services financed by government insurance programs.
how_it_makes_money.franchisor_fees: Franchisors earn initial franchise fees, royalties and sometimes technology, training or marketing fees from operators.

cost_structure.labor: Largest cost category; baseline wages were 50.1% of 2021 revenue and were forecast to reach 53.4% by 2026 because direct-care staffing is hard to automate and labor markets remain tight.
cost_structure.real_estate_and_financing: Land, construction, rent, mortgage interest, renovations and licensing-related buildout are major costs, especially as borrowing and construction costs stayed elevated in 2024-2026.
cost_structure.food_supplies_and_care_inputs: Meals, linens, housekeeping supplies, medical-adjacent consumables, resident activities and maintenance scale with occupancy.
cost_structure.royalties_and_brand_support: Franchisees typically pay upfront franchise fees and ongoing royalties; BeeHive Homes lists a 5% royalty and $75,000 initial franchise fee in 2025-2026 franchise materials.
cost_structure.compliance_and_insurance: State licensing, staff training, background checks, liability insurance, medication protocols and dementia-care compliance add recurring overhead.
cost_structure.profit: Baseline franchise EBIT margin was 14.8% in 2021, but margins are sensitive to staffing ratios, occupancy, insurance and local wage rates.

major_players: BeeHive Homes: residential assisted-living franchise with 200+ homes nationwide and more than 35 years of operating history cited in 2025-2026 franchise materials.
Majestic Residences: residential assisted-living franchise platform that announced the 2025 acquisition of Avendelle Senior Living Franchise, adding 17 operating homes and 6 in development.

Assisted Living Locators: senior-care placement franchise with 155 franchise locations across 39 states in January 2025; adjacent to the residential-care franchise ecosystem rather than a facility operator.
Oasis Senior Advisors: senior-living placement franchise serving families and communities, relevant as a referral channel for residential senior care homes.
Independent local franchisees: the market remains fragmented, with many small residential homes and local owners operating under franchise systems or licensing models.

current_dynamics.demand: Demand is expanding as Baby Boomers age into higher-care years and more families need memory care, medication support and help with activities of daily living.
current_dynamics.supply: New senior-housing construction is constrained; NIC reported Q1 2025 construction starts of 1,076 units in 31 primary markets, the lowest count since Q2 2009, and Q4 2025 inventory growth remained below 1%.
current_dynamics.pricing_power: High occupancy and limited new supply are supporting rent growth, though affordability limits remain because many residents pay privately.
current_dynamics.labor: Staffing remains the operating bottleneck, with caregiver wages, retention, training and state staffing expectations pressuring margins.
current_dynamics.capital: Higher interest rates and construction costs favor asset-light placement franchises and operators that can acquire or convert existing homes rather than build large new facilities.
current_dynamics.regulation: Medicaid access rules, state assisted-living oversight and dementia-care requirements are pushing operators toward better documentation, training and quality systems.

whats_growing: Memory care and dementia-capable residential homes as Alzheimer's prevalence rises; 7.2 million Americans age 65+ had Alzheimer's dementia in 2025.
Small-home assisted-living formats that market higher staff attention and a less institutional feel than large campuses.
Occupancy and revenue per available unit as senior housing occupancy reached 89.1% in Q4 2025 and crossed 90% across primary and secondary markets in Q2 2026.
Franchise and platform consolidation, illustrated by Majestic Residences' 2025 Avendelle acquisition.
Referral and placement franchises that help families navigate assisted living, memory care and senior housing options.
whats_shrinking: Available supply in tight markets, because construction starts and inventory growth remain below historical norms.
Margin cushion for operators that cannot pass through caregiver wage, insurance, food and debt-service costs.
Reliance on broad Medicare coverage for room-and-board costs, since assisted living remains mainly private pay and Medicare generally does not cover custodial residential care.
Standalone low-acuity senior housing value propositions in markets where families increasingly seek care continuity, memory support and medication oversight.
Development appetite for expensive new builds in high-rate markets, favoring acquisitions, conversions and smaller projects.
recent_developments: 2025-01-14: Assisted Living Locators reported 155 franchise locations across 39 states while marketing its senior-care placement franchise model.
2025-02-16: Majestic Residences announced the acquisition of Avendelle Senior Living Franchise, adding 17 operating homes and 6 homes in development.
2025-04-03: NIC reported U.S. senior housing occupancy rose to 87.4% in Q1 2025, with assisted living at 85.8% and construction starts at a post-2009 low.
2026-01-15: NIC reported senior housing occupancy ended 2025 at 89.1%, with assisted living occupancy at 87.7% after 18 consecutive quarters of occupancy gains.
2026-03-12: JLL reported senior-housing rolling four-quarter transaction volume reached $24 billion by year-end 2025, the highest in a decade.
2026-06-25: Census Vintage 2025 estimates showed the U.S. 65+ population reached 64.6 million in July 2025, up 16.2% from April 2020.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but capacity-constrained. The baseline forecast points to about $9.0 billion of franchised residential senior care revenue in 2026, while newer public indicators show demand strengthening faster than new supply. Occupancy above pre-pandemic levels, a rapidly expanding 65+ population and rising dementia prevalence should support pricing and unit growth. The main downside risks are affordability, caregiver shortages, higher financing costs, state-level compliance burdens and reimbursement pressure where Medicaid waiver residents are part of the payer mix. Operators with strong recruiting systems, memory-care protocols, local referral networks and disciplined real-estate models are best positioned.

title: Soybean Processing
one_liner: U.S. soybean processors crush beans into meal, oil, hulls and specialty ingredients, with growth now tied more to biofuels and meal exports than to food-service recovery.
overview: Soybean processing is a mature, capital-intensive manufacturing industry centered on crushing soybeans and separating them into protein meal and oil. The baseline IBISWorld file showed 2021 revenue of $33.4 billion after pandemic disruption, with 2021-2026 revenue forecast to rise at a 1.6% CAGR to $36.1 billion. Public 2025 IBISWorld listing data show the industry had instead expanded sharply through 2023 to $54.3 billion, reflecting high commodity prices and stronger product demand before a 2023 pullback. In 2025-2026, the operating story is record or near-record domestic crush, expanded Midwest and Plains capacity, renewable diesel demand for soybean oil, and larger exportable supplies of soybean meal.

key_stats.crush_volume: 2025/26 U.S. soybean crush forecast: 2.65 billion bushels in USDA June 2026 outlook; USDA July 2025 chart had earlier forecast 2.49 billion bushels for 2025/26
key_stats.crush_share: 2025/26 crush expected to account for about 57% of U.S. soybean production
key_stats.renewable_diesel_capacity: 2025 U.S. renewable diesel and other non-ethanol biofuels capacity: 4.719 billion gallons per year as of Jan. 1, 2025
key_stats.industry_structure: 2025 NOPA members crush more than 98% of U.S. soybeans processed and operate 69-73 soybean and softseed extraction plants, depending on 2025 membership timing

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline estimate: $33.9 billion, derived from the baseline file's 2021 revenue of $33.4 billion and its 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 1.6%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline growth estimate: +1.6%, using the baseline file's 2021-2026 forecast CAGR
baseline_2022.context: 2022 Economic Census reported $60.1 billion in shipments for NAICS 311224 Soybean and Other Oilseed Processing, a broader category than the IBIS soybean-only report

how_it_makes_money: Processors buy soybeans, operate crushing and extraction plants, and sell soybean meal into animal feed and export markets, soybean oil into food, industrial and biofuel markets, and hulls or specialty soy products into feed and ingredient channels. Revenue moves with crush volumes, soybean input prices, meal and oil prices, basis spreads, capacity utilization and export demand.

cost_structure.feedstock_purchases: Soybeans are the dominant cost and the main source of margin volatility; processors try to pass commodity-cost changes through to meal and oil buyers.
cost_structure.energy_and_utilities: Crushing, extraction, refining and drying require meaningful power, heat, solvent handling and logistics costs.
cost_structure.labor: Baseline 2021 wages were $495 million, about 1.5% of 2021 revenue, reflecting a capital-intensive plant model.
cost_structure.depreciation_and_maintenance: Large solvent-extraction plants, storage, rail/truck loading and environmental controls create high fixed costs and favor high utilization.
cost_structure.profitability: Baseline 2021 profit margin was 6.5%; a public 2026 South Dakota Soybean Processors filing showed 2025 cost of revenues at 95.1% of revenue, illustrating thin gross spreads at plant level.

current_dynamics: Domestic crush is expanding because soybean oil has become a strategic feedstock for biomass-based diesel while soybean meal demand is supported by livestock feed and exports. The buildout creates more local demand for Midwestern and Plains soybeans, but it also increases the need to clear larger meal supplies into domestic feed and export markets. Biofuel policy, 45Z tax-credit rules, RFS volumes, low-carbon fuel standards, imported feedstock treatment and South American competition are now central to margins.
whats_growing: Domestic soybean crush volumes, new crushing capacity in states such as North Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin and Ohio, soybean oil demand for renewable diesel and SAF-linked clean fuels, and soybean meal exports as extra meal is produced alongside oil.
whats_shrinking: The share of U.S. soybeans exported whole has declined as more beans are crushed domestically; soybean oil available for traditional food, feed, industrial and export channels is pressured by biofuel demand; U.S. global share in soybean and soy product exports remains under pressure from Brazil and Argentina.
recent_developments: 2025-01-10: Treasury and IRS released initial guidance for the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit, shaping demand for qualifying domestic clean-fuel feedstocks.
2025-07-01: USDA ERS reported 2025/26 U.S. soybean crush was forecast to rise nearly 3% to a record 2.49 billion bushels and reach 57% of U.S. production.
2025-07-02: NOPA added Platinum Crush, whose Alta, Iowa plant began operations in 2024 with 40 million bushels of annual capacity.
2025-09-26: EIA reported U.S. renewable diesel and other non-ethanol biofuels capacity of 4.719 billion gallons per year as of Jan. 1, 2025.
2026-03-27: EPA finalized 2026 and 2027 RFS standards, including biomass-based diesel totals of 9.07 billion RINs for 2026 and 9.20 billion RINs for 2027 after SRE reallocation.
2026-07-15: USDA ERS reported 2026/27 U.S. soybean production was forecast at a record 4.5 billion bushels, with the soybean crush forecast unchanged and exports raised.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is constructive for physical volumes but mixed for margins. Crush capacity additions and biofuel mandates support plant utilization, while 45Z and RFS rules favor domestic feedstocks after 2025. The risk is that rapid capacity growth outpaces soybean oil demand or leaves excess soybean meal chasing export markets, especially as Brazil and Argentina expand production and processing. Revenue may remain volatile because soybean and product prices can move more than underlying tons processed.

title: Vending Machine Operators in the US
one_liner: Traditional vending has recovered in dollars, but growth is being pulled toward cashless, data-driven machines and adjacent micro markets.
overview: This industry consists of businesses that own, stock and service vending machines selling packaged food, snacks, cold and hot beverages and other merchandise. The baseline IBISWorld file described a 2022 rebound from COVID-19 disruption, with revenue rising 3.8% in 2022 to $10.171 billion in 2022 dollars, but also characterized the industry as mature to declining because of falling soft-drink consumption, stricter school nutrition rules, convenience-store competition and micro-market substitution. Current data show the channel has continued to recover in nominal terms: BLS/FRED sectoral output for NAICS 4542 reached $11.027 billion in 2025, up from $10.559 billion in 2024. The strategic issue is that operators increasingly sell a broader convenience-services bundle rather than standalone machines: NAMA's 2026 census estimated the broader US convenience-services industry at $31.1 billion in 2025, including vending, micro markets, office coffee and pantry services.

key_stats.market_size: $11.027 billion in 2025 BLS/FRED sectoral output for Retail Trade: Vending Machine Operators, NAICS 4542
key_stats.growth: 4.4% nominal year-over-year growth in 2025, from $10.559 billion in 2024 to $11.027 billion in 2025
key_stats.employment: 42,600 jobs in 2025 according to BLS/FRED annual employment for NAICS 4542
key_stats.business_count: 17,129 businesses in 2025 according to IBISWorld's April 2025 public industry statistics page
key_stats.business_count_growth: -1.8% in 2025 according to IBISWorld's April 2025 public industry statistics page
key_stats.broader_channel_size: $31.1 billion in 2025 US convenience-services revenue, including vending, micro markets, office coffee and pantry, according to NAMA Foundation data released in 2026
key_stats.broader_channel_growth: 8.1% average annual growth from 2023 to 2025 for US convenience services according to the 2026 NAMA Foundation census release

baseline_2022.market_size: $10.171 billion in 2022 revenue, in 2022 dollars, from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.growth: 0.8% annualized revenue growth over 2017-2022 and 3.8% revenue growth in 2022 from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.profit: $437 million in 2022 profit from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 4.3% of 2022 revenue from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.establishments: 19,564 establishments in 2022 from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.enterprises: 18,883 enterprises in 2022 from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.employment: 52,136 workers in 2022 from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.wages: $1.606 billion in 2022 wages from the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix in the baseline file: food and snacks 32.8%, cold beverages 23.0%, other products 17.4%, candy 14.8%, healthy items 8.2%, hot beverages 3.8%

how_it_makes_money: Operators place machines in workplaces, schools, hospitals, public buildings, factories, travel locations and other high-traffic sites, then earn retail sales from stocked products. Revenue is driven by machine count, location quality, foot traffic, product mix, pricing, payment acceptance and route efficiency. Many operators also use the same sales force, warehouse and route infrastructure to sell micro markets, office coffee and pantry services, although those adjacent lines are broader than the traditional vending-machine operator definition.

cost_structure.largest_costs: Product purchases from beverage, snack, candy, prepared-food and grocery wholesalers are the main variable cost, followed by labor for route drivers, warehouse staff, merchandising, machine maintenance and account management.
cost_structure.baseline_profit_margin: 4.3% in 2022 from the baseline IBISWorld file, reflecting low margin pressure after COVID-19 demand losses and higher sanitation and operating costs.
cost_structure.baseline_wages: $1.606 billion in 2022 wages from the baseline IBISWorld file, equal to about 15.8% of 2022 revenue.
cost_structure.other_costs: Machine depreciation or leasing, vehicle fuel and maintenance, commissions or revenue shares paid to host locations, payment-processing fees, telemetry software, insurance, spoilage for perishable items, utilities for refrigerated equipment and repairs.
cost_structure.margin_pressure: 2024-2025 food and beverage price increases, card fees and equipment upgrades pushed operators to raise prices, consolidate routes and use telemetry, prekitting and cashless systems to protect margins.

major_players: Regional independent vending and micro-market operators
current_dynamics: The core vending channel is growing in nominal dollars but not as strongly as the broader unattended retail ecosystem. BLS/FRED shows 2025 sectoral output of $11.027 billion, while NAMA's broader convenience-services census puts 2025 revenue at $31.1 billion because operators are increasingly mixing vending with micro markets, smart coolers, office coffee and pantry programs. Cashless payments, mobile wallets, remote inventory monitoring, smart coolers and AI-assisted route analytics are becoming standard expectations, especially in workplaces, healthcare, education, residential and hospitality locations. At the same time, the number of businesses continues to fall, with IBISWorld's public 2025 figure showing 17,129 operators, down 1.8% from 2024.
whats_growing: Cashless and mobile-enabled machines, connected telemetry, micro markets, smart coolers, better-for-you snacks, fresh food, protein products, low- and no-sugar beverages, workplace amenity accounts, healthcare and residential locations, and multi-format operators that can offer vending, markets, coffee and pantry under one contract.
whats_shrinking: Standalone cash-only machines, soda-heavy assortments, low-traffic office locations, small operators without route density or purchasing scale, school vending constrained by nutrition rules, and legacy machines that cannot support card, mobile, telemetry or remote merchandising.
recent_developments: 2025-04: IBISWorld's public statistics page listed 17,129 US vending-machine-operator businesses in 2025, down 1.8% from 2024.
2025-05-12: NAMA said its 2025 trade show drew more than 5,200 professionals, its highest attendance in more than two decades, with focus on unattended retail, micro markets, AI and automation.
2025-06-09: NAMA Foundation reported the broader US convenience-services industry generated $40.04 billion in annual economic impact and supported 165,300 jobs.
2025-07-16: Vending Market Watch reported 2024 vending and micro-market sales rose 30% to $33.85 billion in its State of the Vending and Micro Market Industry coverage.
2026-03-20: NAMA Foundation released its 2024-2025 State of Convenience Services census, estimating 2025 convenience-services revenue at $31.1 billion and 8.1% average annual growth since 2023.
2026-06-03: BLS/FRED updated annual vending-machine-operator sectoral output, showing 2025 output of $11.027 billion and 2025 employment of 42,600 jobs.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is modest for traditional vending but stronger for operators that reposition as unattended retail and workplace-refreshment providers. Nominal 2025 growth was positive, but BLS productivity data also point to labor rationalization, and IBISWorld's 2025 public business-count data show continued operator contraction. Growth should come from higher prices, upgraded connected machines, broader product assortments and new placements in healthcare, residential, manufacturing, education and hospitality. The main constraints are weak low-traffic locations, competition from convenience stores and employer-funded food programs, rising product costs, payment fees, capital requirements and the continued shift of revenue into micro markets that may sit outside the narrow vending category.
themes: Micro markets blur the industry boundary
Route density and telemetry drive margins
Smart coolers and connected machines expand unattended retail
one_sentence: US vending machine operators remain a large unattended retail channel, with 2025 BLS sectoral output of $11.027 billion, but low concentration, fewer operators, healthier product demand and micro-market substitution keep the core category structurally pressured.

title: Video Postproduction Services in the US
one_liner: US video postproduction is a fragmented services market tied to streaming, advertising video, film and TV production, with growth in digital formats offset by production cuts, insourcing and AI pressure.
overview: Video postproduction services prepare filmed or recorded video for distribution through editing, visual effects, animation, color correction, restoration, subtitling, captioning, sound editing, format conversion and duplication. The industry excludes postproduction done in-house by studios, networks, streamers and production companies. The 2022 baseline showed a mature, fragmented industry with low concentration, low entry barriers, high competition and high technology change. The 2025-2026 market remains structurally attractive where work is complex, fast-turnaround or platform-specific, but the volume environment is uneven because studios and streamers have reduced series orders, shifted production locations, increased use of in-house teams and tested generative-AI workflows.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US revenue of about $5.6 billion, using the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $5.387 billion and updated 2025 demand signals from advertising, box office and production activity
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated revenue growth roughly 0% to 2% year over year; 2022-2027 baseline forecast CAGR was 2.2%
key_stats.employment: 2022 baseline employment was 53,513 workers; 2026 broader NAICS 512 motion picture and sound recording employment was 321,700 in June 2026, down from 336,600 in March 2026
key_stats.establishments: 2022 baseline establishments were 22,929; 2025 broader NAICS 512 private establishments were 40,561 in Q4 2025
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022 baseline EBIT margin was 6.5%; 2027 baseline forecast margin was 6.2%
key_stats.digital_video_ad_spend: US digital video ad spend grew 18% in 2024 to $64 billion and was projected by IAB to reach about $72 billion in 2025

baseline_2022.growth: Revenue declined at a 3.1% annualized rate over 2017-2022, with 2022 revenue up 1.7% as pandemic-delayed production resumed
baseline_2022.profit: $350 million in 2022 profit, equal to a 6.5% margin

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn project fees, retainers and hourly or day rates from film producers, TV producers, streamers, ad agencies, brands, distributors and content owners. Revenue comes from nonlinear editing, VFX and animation, finishing, color grading, digital restoration, localization, subtitling, captioning, sound design, conforming, mastering, delivery-version creation and archive conversion. Larger vendors win complex studio and streamer work, while freelancers and boutiques compete on specialized editing, social-video formatting, quick-turn ads and lower-budget productions.

cost_structure.labor: Very high; the 2022 baseline wage bill of $2.995 billion equaled about 55.6% of revenue, reflecting editors, colorists, VFX artists, sound engineers, producers and technical supervisors
cost_structure.profit: 6.5% of revenue in 2022 baseline, with pressure from freelancer competition, client bargaining power and VFX bid overruns
cost_structure.software_cloud_and_rendering: Rising share in 2025-2026 due to subscription editing suites, cloud collaboration, storage, GPU rendering and cybersecurity requirements
cost_structure.rent_and_facilities: Moderate; premium finishing rooms, screening rooms and sound stages remain important, but remote workflows reduce some facility needs
cost_structure.equipment_depreciation: Moderate; workstations, storage, color suites, sound equipment and display systems require frequent refreshes
cost_structure.purchases_and_outsourcing: Project-dependent; boutiques subcontract VFX, localization, music, Foley, render capacity and overflow editing

major_players: No single company dominates the US industry; the baseline describes low market concentration and a large freelancer base
current_dynamics: The market is being pulled in opposite directions. Digital video advertising and CTV are expanding, creating more short-form, versioned and platform-specific finishing work. Streaming remains a major content spender, but profitability pressure has made buyers more selective, with fewer scripted series, shorter orders and tighter post budgets. Theatrical box office improved from 2020 lows but remained below 2019, limiting some premium film-driven work. Los Angeles production weakness in 2024-2025 reduced local project flow, although California's expanded film and TV tax credit may support later recovery. Generative AI is accelerating rotoscoping, cleanup, localization, rough cuts and asset generation, improving productivity but threatening lower-complexity labor and pricing.
whats_growing: CTV, social video and online video ad finishing, with US digital video ad spend projected at about $72 billion in 2025
Versioning, localization, captioning and aspect-ratio conversion for streaming, social platforms and global releases
Complex VFX, animation, color, restoration and premium finishing that studios cannot easily commoditize
Cloud review, remote editorial, virtual production handoff and AI-assisted post workflows
Sports, live-event and creator-led video packages for streaming platforms
whats_shrinking: Linear editing, tape-based workflows and physical duplication
Cable-network-driven postproduction tied to declining pay-TV subscriptions
Routine editing, subtitling, cleanup and simple graphics that can be automated or brought in-house
Some Los Angeles-based scripted and commercial production volumes, which weakened in 2024 and 2025
Standalone VFX vendors with thin margins, fixed overhead and heavy dependence on studio tentpoles
recent_developments: 2025-01: FilmLA reported Greater Los Angeles on-location production fell 5.6% in 2024 to 23,480 shoot days, the second-lowest annual level after 2020
2025-04: IAB projected US digital video ad spend would rise 14% in 2025 to about $72 billion after 18% growth in 2024

outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is modestly positive but more selective than the 2022 baseline forecast. Revenue should grow where vendors serve digital video advertising, streaming localization, premium finishing, restoration and complex VFX, but lower production volumes, studio insourcing and AI-assisted workflows will cap pricing power. Firms with scalable cloud pipelines, strong client relationships and specialized creative talent should gain share, while small providers focused on commodity editing or duplication face margin compression. A reasonable 2026 view is low-single-digit growth from a roughly $5.6 billion 2025 base, assuming advertising remains resilient and production incentives begin converting into active shoots.
one_sentence: In 2025-2026, video postproduction demand is being supported by digital video advertising and streaming content spend, but constrained by lower US scripted production volumes, weak theatrical recovery versus 2019 and margin pressure in VFX-heavy work.

title: Waste-to-Energy Plant Operation
one_liner: US waste-to-energy operators earn most of their money from municipal waste-disposal contracts, with power sales and recovered metals adding upside but not enough to offset flat capacity and tighter emissions rules.
overview: This industry covers private operators of US waste-to-energy plants, including privately owned facilities and private operation of municipal plants. Plants burn post-recycled municipal solid waste, mostly through mass-burn systems, to produce steam, electricity and recoverable metals while charging disposal or service fees. The business is structurally defensive because municipalities need disposal capacity, especially in dense Northeast markets with limited landfill space, but it is not a high-growth power segment. EIA reported 60 operating US WTE electric plants with 2,051 MW at the beginning of 2022, while EPA's 2026 MSW combustion page cites 75 energy-recovery combustion facilities in 25 states. The sector is being pulled in two directions: landfill-diversion and methane concerns support the service, while source reduction, recycling policy, environmental-justice scrutiny and 2026 EPA municipal waste combustor standards raise the hurdle for older assets.

key_stats.market_size: 2024 US WTE market value estimated at about $5.85 billion, calculated from GlobalData's 2024 North America WTE revenue of $7.2426 billion and its 80.7% US share; this is broader than the baseline private plant-operation scope.
key_stats.growth: 2019-2024 North America WTE market value CAGR was 2.9%; EIA preliminary biogenic MSW consumption for electricity and useful thermal output fell from 15.247 million tons in 2024 to 14.489 million tons in 2025, a 5.0% decline.
key_stats.facilities: 2022 EIA counted 60 operating US WTE electric plants with 2,051 MW; EPA's 2026 MSW combustion page cites 75 US energy-recovery combustion facilities in 25 states.
key_stats.generation: 2022 EIA reported US WTE facilities consumed 16.0 million tons of biogenic waste and 10.3 million tons of non-biogenic waste; EIA described WTE as roughly 14,000 GWh per year over the prior decade and less than 1% of US electricity generation.
key_stats.unit_economics: 2026 EPA states a typical WTE plant generates about 550 kWh per ton of waste, with electricity revenue often $20-$30 per ton at $0.04/kWh.
key_stats.regulation: EPA finalized revised large municipal waste combustor standards on March 5, 2026, effective May 11, 2026.

baseline_2022.market_size: About $1.38 billion in 2022 for the narrower IBIS private plant-operation scope, derived from the baseline 2021 revenue of $1.36 billion and its 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 1.1%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 implied growth of about 1.1% under the baseline 2021-2026 forecast.
baseline_2022.establishments: Baseline projected a mostly flat base from 64 private establishments in 2021 toward modest growth by 2026.
baseline_2022.employment: Baseline expected employment to recover from 2,423 workers in 2021 toward about 2,500 by 2026.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: Baseline 2021 profit margin was 8.7%, with limited margin expansion expected because of high operating and compliance costs.

how_it_makes_money: Operators collect municipal or hauler tipping fees and long-term service payments for accepting post-recycled MSW; sell electricity, steam or renewable attributes where eligible; recover ferrous and non-ferrous metals from ash; and sometimes earn contract operations fees, special-waste fees or environmental-credit revenue. Tipping fees are typically the anchor revenue stream, while power and metals add commodity-sensitive upside.
cost_structure: Major 2025-2026 costs are labor for 24/7 operations, boiler and turbine maintenance, air-pollution-control reagents and monitoring, ash handling and landfill disposal, insurance, property taxes, debt service and major capital repairs. Baseline 2021 wages were $188 million, about 13.8% of $1.36 billion revenue, and profit margin was 8.7%. EPA's 2026 large municipal waste combustor rule adds compliance, reporting and control-technology pressure for affected units.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 operating environment is stable but less expansive than global WTE forecasts imply. Waste disposal demand is durable, landfill capacity remains tight in parts of the Northeast and Florida, and higher electricity demand improves the value of baseload output. At the same time, EIA preliminary data show biogenic MSW consumption for electricity and useful thermal output declined 5.0% in 2025, and 2026 rolling 12-month consumption through April was below the comparable 2025 period. Several older facilities have closed or announced closures as state incentives, local air rules and emissions-control costs change project economics.
whats_growing: Non-incineration waste-diversion services, recovered metals optimization, corporate zero-waste services, wastewater and specialty-waste offerings at diversified operators, landfill-avoidance demand in dense markets, and compliance-related retrofit work are growing. Broader global WTE market estimates remain positive for 2025-2031, especially outside the US, but US combustion capacity growth is selective.
whats_shrinking: Legacy incinerator capacity in states that removed renewable or diversion credits is shrinking, including California and Oregon closures in 2024. Biogenic MSW consumption for energy fell from 15.247 million tons in 2024 to 14.489 million tons in 2025. Public tolerance for new mass-burn facilities remains limited, and recycling/source-reduction policies can reduce available feedstock over time.
recent_developments: 2024-04-16: Covanta announced its rebrand to Reworld after expanding beyond legacy waste-to-energy into broader sustainable waste services.
2024-10-08: Reworld confirmed plans to wind down the Stanislaus County facility, California's last operating MSW incinerator, with operations ending in late 2024.
2024-12-31: Reworld Marion in Oregon ended waste-incineration operations after state-level emissions and reporting requirements tightened.
2025-04-07: WIN Waste Saugus reported a 2024 annual air-monitoring review that found the WTE plant and monofill met applicable air-compliance criteria.
2026-03-05: EPA finalized updated large municipal waste combustor standards, revising emissions limits and recordkeeping requirements for affected WTE units.
2026-08-07: WIN Waste's Hudson Falls, New York plant was reported to be closing by the end of 2026 after local clean-air restrictions and long-running community opposition.
outlook: Through 2026-2029, US WTE plant operation should remain a mature, contract-driven niche rather than a broad buildout market. Revenue should be supported by municipal disposal needs, inflation-linked service fees, tighter landfill capacity in selected regions and electricity demand growth, but physical throughput and generation capacity are likely to stay flat to down as aging facilities face retrofit decisions. The best-positioned operators are those with long-term municipal contracts, strong air-compliance performance, metals-recovery systems and broader waste-services platforms that can shift volume among WTE, recycling, transfer and disposal options.
themes: Baseload renewable or partially renewable power
one_sentence: Waste-to-energy plant operators run high-capital, heavily regulated combustion facilities that reduce landfill volumes and produce baseload electricity, but the US market remains mature, politically contested and exposed to weaker waste-throughput trends, lower renewable-credit support and rising compliance costs.
